name: Jean-Marie Lehn
milestone_by_age_26: Ineligible: PhD in 1963 at age 24 and CNRS researcher position by 26, but no seminal publication or notable discovery by age 26. His Nobel-winning work on cryptands and supramolecular chemistry began around 1966-1968 (age 27-29).
early_history_summary: Lehn grew up in Rosheim, Alsace, son of a baker-turned-organist. He studied at the University of Strasbourg, earned his PhD in 1963 under Guy Ourisson on conformational studies of triterpenes, and did a postdoc at Harvard with R.B. Woodward on vitamin B12 synthesis in 1964 before returning to Strasbourg.
family_context_summary: Father was a baker who became an organist; mother kept the house and shop. Working-class family in post-war Alsace.
evidence_summary: Lehn earned his PhD at 24 and was a CNRS researcher by 26, but his Nobel-winning supramolecular chemistry work came later (age 27+). A PhD alone without a seminal publication or discovery does not qualify as a material milestone.

name: Rupert Murdoch
milestone_by_age_26: Inherited and took over The News, an Adelaide newspaper, at age 22 in 1953 after his father's death, and by age 26 had expanded the business to Perth (Sunday Times, 1956) and multiple other newspapers across Australia.
early_history_summary: Murdoch was born in Melbourne to Sir Keith Murdoch, a prominent newspaper magnate and chairman of Herald and Weekly Times. He was groomed by his father to take over the family business, attending Geelong Grammar and Oxford University. After his father died in 1952, Murdoch returned to Adelaide at age 21 to take charge of News Limited, turning the small Adelaide News into a success and rapidly expanding through acquisitions.
family_context_summary: Son of Sir Keith Murdoch, Australia's most prominent newspaper magnate, and Dame Elisabeth Greene. Raised in a wealthy media family with direct access to the newspaper industry.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a war correspondent turned regional newspaper magnate who owned newspapers in Adelaide, a radio station, and chaired the Herald and Weekly Times publishing company. He actively groomed Rupert for the media business, introducing him to Fleet Street figures.
primary_early_advantage_tags: inherited newspaper, father's media empire, Fleet Street connections, family business succession
evidence_summary: Murdoch inherited News Limited and its Adelaide newspaper at age 22 after his father's death in 1952. His father, Sir Keith Murdoch, was Australia's leading newspaper magnate and had groomed Rupert for the role, introducing him to Fleet Street editors and arranging stints at the Birmingham Gazette and Daily Express. By 26, Murdoch had expanded to Perth and was building a multi-city newspaper group, leveraging inherited distribution, capital, and industry networks.

name: Svante Pääbo
milestone_by_age_26: Ineligible: By age 26 (1981), Pääbo was just beginning his PhD studies at Uppsala University. His seminal mummy DNA work was published in Nature in 1985 (age 30), and his PhD was completed in 1986 (age 31). No material milestone by 26.
early_history_summary: Pääbo studied humanities and medicine at Uppsala University from 1975, including Egyptology and history of science, before beginning full-time PhD research in cell biology in 1981. His groundbreaking ancient DNA work on Egyptian mummies came as a side project during his PhD, published in 1985.
evidence_summary: Pääbo was still in early PhD studies by age 26, having spent years on humanities and medical coursework. His pioneering ancient DNA research and Nature publication came at age 30, well after the age-26 cutoff.

name: Bob Kahn
milestone_by_age_26: Ineligible: PhD from Princeton in 1964 at age 26, followed by MIT assistant professorship. The ARPANET system design work at BBN began in 1966 (age 28), and the seminal TCP/IP paper was published in 1974 (age 36). PhD alone is not a material milestone.
early_history_summary: Kahn earned a BEE from City College of New York in 1960, then MA and PhD from Princeton in 1962 and 1964. He worked at Bell Labs during his studies, then became an assistant professor at MIT before taking a leave of absence to join BBN in 1966, where he led the system design of the ARPANET.
evidence_summary: Kahn completed his PhD at 26 and joined MIT as assistant professor, but his defining work on ARPANET and TCP/IP came years later (1966 and 1974 respectively). No seminal publication, product, or discovery by age 26.

name: Bernie Madoff
milestone_by_age_26: Founded Bernard L. Madoff Investment Securities LLC in 1960 at age 22, using $5,000 in personal savings and $50,000 borrowed from his in-laws, establishing a legitimate market-making and brokerage firm that grew into the sixth-largest market maker in S&P 500 stocks.
early_history_summary: Madoff grew up in Queens, New York, the son of a plumber-turned-stockbroker. He graduated from Far Rockaway High School in 1956, attended the University of Alabama for one year, then transferred to Hofstra University, earning a bachelor's in political science in 1960. He briefly attended Brooklyn Law School before founding his investment firm with savings from lifeguarding and sprinkler installation work, plus loans from his father-in-law, a successful accountant who referred clients.
family_context_summary: Son of Ralph Madoff, a plumber who later entered the financial industry and co-founded Gibraltar Securities (which was shut down by the SEC), and Sylvia Madoff. Middle-class upbringing in Queens, New York.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father worked as a plumber before entering the financial industry with his wife, founding Gibraltar Securities. This gave Madoff some early exposure to the finance world, though the firm was ultimately forced to close by the SEC.
primary_early_advantage_tags: father-in-law's client referrals, Wall Street proximity, family finance exposure, middle-class outsider drive
evidence_summary: Madoff founded his investment firm at age 22 in 1960, capitalizing on $5,000 in personal savings and $50,000 borrowed from his in-laws. His father-in-law, a successful accountant, referred early clients. His father had transitioned from plumbing to finance, founding Gibraltar Securities, giving Madoff some domain exposure. The firm grew into a major market maker, though Madoff's later infamy stemmed from the Ponzi scheme.

name: Leon Cooper
milestone_by_age_26: Published the seminal paper 'Bound Electron Pairs in a Degenerate Fermi Gas' in Physical Review in November 1956 at age 26, introducing the concept of Cooper pairs that became foundational to the BCS theory of superconductivity and earned the 1972 Nobel Prize in Physics.
early_history_summary: Cooper was born in the Bronx to an immigrant family; his father from Belarus and mother from Poland (who died when he was seven). He attended the Bronx High School of Science, where he won the Westinghouse Science Talent Search, then Columbia University, earning his BA in 1951, MA in 1953, and PhD in 1954 under Robert Serber. After a postdoc at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, he joined John Bardeen at the University of Illinois in 1955 as a research associate, where he developed the Cooper pair concept.
family_context_summary: Son of Irving Kupchik (from Belarus, immigrated after the Russian Revolution) and Anna Zola (from Poland, who died when Leon was seven). His father remarried and changed the family surname to Cooper. Immigrant working-class background.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources. No evidence of parental scientific or academic expertise.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Bronx High School of Science, Columbia University, IAS Princeton, Bardeen collaboration, Westinghouse prize
evidence_summary: Cooper published his seminal Cooper pairs paper at age 26 in November 1956, work that became the foundation of BCS theory and earned the 1972 Nobel Prize. His path ran through Bronx High School of Science (where he won the Westinghouse Science Talent Search), Columbia University (PhD at 24), IAS Princeton, and the University of Illinois where he collaborated with John Bardeen. His immigrant background and early loss of his mother suggest modest family advantages, with his acceleration driven primarily by elite institutional pipelines and an exceptional collaboration with Bardeen and Schrieffer.

name: Vince McMahon
milestone_by_age_26: Ineligible: By age 26 (1971), McMahon was working as a commentator/announcer for his father's WWWF promotion. He did not buy the company until 1982 (age 37) and did not achieve commercial success as a promoter until WrestleMania in 1985 (age 40). No material milestone by 26.
early_history_summary: McMahon was born in Pinehurst, North Carolina, and did not meet his father, wrestling promoter Vincent J. McMahon, until age 12. He graduated from East Carolina University with a business degree in 1968 and worked as a traveling salesman before joining his father's World Wide Wrestling Federation as an announcer in 1969. He wanted to be a wrestler but his father prohibited it.
family_context_summary: Son of Vincent J. McMahon, a wrestling promoter who ran Capitol Wrestling Corporation (later WWWF). Father left the family when Vince was an infant; they reconnected when Vince was 12. Grandfather Jess McMahon was also a boxing and wrestling promoter.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father and grandfather were both wrestling promoters, but Vince did not grow up with his father and had limited early exposure to the business until age 12. He joined the family business as an announcer at 24 but did not assume control until 37.
evidence_summary: By age 26, McMahon was only an announcer for his father's wrestling promotion. His material milestone of acquiring and transforming the company came at age 37 in 1982, well after the age-26 cutoff.

name: Sepp Blatter
milestone_by_age_26: Ineligible: By age 26 (1962), Blatter was working as head of public relations for tourism in the canton of Valais. His first significant sports administration role came as Secretary General of the Swiss Ice Hockey Federation in 1964 (age 28), and he joined FIFA as technical director in 1975 (age 39). No material milestone by 26.
early_history_summary: Blatter was born in Visp, Switzerland, to a modest family; his father worked in a chemical plant. He studied business administration and economics at the University of Lausanne, served in the Swiss militia army rising to colonel, and worked in public relations for the Valais tourist board (1959-1964) before moving to sports administration.
family_context_summary: Born to a modest family in the Alpine town of Visp; father worked in a vast chemical plant. Blatter reportedly had the only professional-quality football in his school playground.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources. No evidence of parental sports administration or business expertise.
evidence_summary: Blatter was working in tourism PR by age 26, with his first sports administration role (Swiss Ice Hockey Federation) coming at 28 and FIFA at 39. No material milestone by 26.

name: Warren Buffett
milestone_by_age_26: Founded Buffett Partnership Ltd. in May 1956 at age 25, pooling $105,000 from seven limited partners (all family and personal connections) to launch an investment partnership that eventually grew into Berkshire Hathaway, one of the world's largest conglomerates.
early_history_summary: Buffett was born in Omaha, Nebraska, the son of U.S. Congressman Howard Buffett. He displayed an intense interest in business from childhood, selling gum door-to-door, delivering newspapers, and buying his first stock at age 11. He bought a 40-acre farm at 14 and had $9,800 in savings by college graduation. After attending Wharton and graduating from the University of Nebraska at 19, he earned an MS from Columbia Business School under Ben Graham, then worked at Graham-Newman Corp. from 1954 to 1956 before founding his partnership with $174,000 in personal savings.
family_context_summary: Son of U.S. Congressman Howard Buffett and Leila Stahl Buffett. Grew up in a politically connected, upper-middle-class household in Omaha and Washington, D.C. Father was an investment salesman before entering Congress.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father Howard Buffett was a U.S. Congressman and investment salesman who actively cultivated Warren's interest in business and investing, taking him to visit the New York Stock Exchange at age 10 and directing him toward formal education in the field. Father's brokerage office provided Warren's earliest exposure to the stock market.
primary_early_advantage_tags: father's brokerage, Ben Graham mentorship, early investing from age 11, Columbia Business School, congressional family
evidence_summary: Buffett founded his investment partnership at age 25 in 1956, leveraging years of investing experience that began at age 11, mentorship from Ben Graham at Columbia and Graham-Newman, and $174,000 in personal savings. His father, Congressman Howard Buffett, actively cultivated his interest in business and provided access to the brokerage world. The initial partnership capital came entirely from family and personal connections, reflecting strong inherited networks rather than market-proven distribution.

name: Peter J. Ratcliffe
milestone_by_age_26: Ineligible: By age 26 (1980), Ratcliffe was a medical trainee in nephrology at Oxford. His MD degree was completed in 1987 (age 33), his hypoxia biology lab was established in 1990 (age 36), and the Nobel Prize came in 2019. No material milestone by 26.
early_history_summary: Ratcliffe grew up in northwest England and attended Lancaster Royal Grammar School. He studied medicine at Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge and St. Bartholomew's Hospital, London, before moving to Oxford in 1978 to train in renal medicine. His research career developed slowly, beginning with medical case reports before progressing to oxygen-sensing research.
family_context_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources. Grew up in northwest England; attended Lancaster Royal Grammar School, a state grammar school.
evidence_summary: Ratcliffe was a medical trainee by age 26 with no notable publications or discoveries. His Nobel-winning oxygen-sensing research began years later, with his lab established at age 36 in 1990.

name: Barry Barish
milestone_by_age_26: Ineligible: PhD from UC Berkeley in 1962 at age 26, followed by a research fellowship. His Nobel-winning LIGO work began in 1994 (age 58). No seminal publication, notable product, or significant discovery by age 26. PhD alone is not a material milestone.
early_history_summary: Barish was born in Omaha, Nebraska, to Eastern European Jewish immigrant families. He entered UC Berkeley as an engineering student but switched to physics, earning his BA in 1957 and PhD in experimental high energy physics in 1962. He did research fellowships at Berkeley and then joined Caltech in 1963 as part of a particle physics effort.
family_context_summary: Both parents' families immigrated to the U.S. from small shtetls in Eastern Europe (Ukraine/Belarus area) around the turn of the 20th century. Family background not well documented; apparently not distinguished.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources. No evidence of parental scientific or academic expertise.
evidence_summary: Barish completed his PhD at age 26 and took a research fellowship, but his Nobel-winning LIGO leadership came decades later at age 58. No material milestone by 26.

name: Douglas Osheroff
milestone_by_age_26: Co-discovered superfluidity in helium-3 in November 1971 at age 26 as a graduate student at Cornell, making the key experimental observations of phase transitions in helium-3 at ultra-low temperatures. The first paper was published in Physical Review Letters in April 1972, and the discovery earned the 1996 Nobel Prize in Physics.
early_history_summary: Osheroff was born in Aberdeen, Washington, to a working-class family; his father was the son of Jewish immigrants from Russia and his mother was a nurse and daughter of Slovak immigrants. As a teenager he built a 100,000-volt X-ray machine, showing early experimental aptitude. He earned his BS from Caltech in 1967, where he attended lectures by Richard Feynman, then joined Cornell's low-temperature physics laboratory as a graduate student under David Lee, where he made the critical observations leading to the discovery of superfluid helium-3.
family_context_summary: Father was the son of Jewish immigrants from Russia; mother was a nurse and daughter of Slovak immigrants. Working-class background in Aberdeen, Washington, a logging town.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources. No evidence of parental scientific or academic expertise.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Caltech, Cornell low-temperature lab, Lee and Richardson collaboration, Feynman lectures, early experimental aptitude
evidence_summary: Osheroff co-discovered superfluidity in helium-3 at age 26 as a Cornell graduate student, making the critical experimental observations in November 1971 that led to the 1996 Nobel Prize. His path ran through Caltech (BS 1967, Feynman lectures) and Cornell's low-temperature physics lab, where he worked under David Lee with Robert Richardson. His working-class immigrant background offered few inherited advantages; his acceleration came from elite institutional access and an exceptional collaboration with two senior physicists who became his Nobel co-laureates.
